summary: The respondent assessee was assessed to wealth tax for the assessment years 1965 66, 1966 67 and 1967 68 (the respective valuation dates being March 31, 1965 and March 31, 1967 respectively. The Wealth Tax Officer included a sum of Rs. 1,50,000/- on accrual basis (though not realised) on the outstandings of the money lending business, the accounts of the assessee being maintained on cash basis basis. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner rejected the assessee 's appeal and held that accrued interest was liable to be included in the wealth tax assessments of the assessee. The Appellate Tribunal held that accrued Interest was liable to tax under the Wealth Tax Act for a reference of the cases to this Court in view of the conflict of opinion between the Orissa High Court and the Andhra Pradesh High Court. The High Court held that accrued interests were liable to be excluded in the wealth Tax assessments of the respondent assessee. The Revenue appealed to this Court. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The High Court was in error in holding that accrued interest is liable to be added in the wealthtax assessments of the appellant. [310 G] The High Court in Commissioner of Wealth Tax, A.P. I vs Pachigolla Narasimha Rao (Orissa) (supra) and by the Karnataka High Court in A. T. In the result, the question is answered in the affirmative, in favour of the Revenue and against the assessee. [310 A B] The High court in Commissioner of Income Tax, A..P. I. vs Pachigtta Narasimha Rao(Orissa) (2) and the Calcutta High Court in Dipti Kumar Basu vs Commissioner of Wealth tax, West Bengal(2) and by Karnataka High Court, in A. P. I. (2) has held that accruedinterest was liable to include in the net wealth of the assessee, if he were alive. [310 F] The High 'Court in Commissioner of wealth Tax, A P. I vs Mysyaraju Badreenarayana Moorthy Raju (Orissa) and by this Court in Commissioner Of Wealth Tax, West Bengal vs VysyarajuBadreenarayana moorthy Raju ( Orissa) (supra), has held that even though the assets to be considered are not circumscribed by any consideration of the particular system of accounting adopted by the assessee, the asset would fetch if sold in the open market on the valuation date. [310 C] The High "Court" in the instant case has fixed upon the last day of the income tax "previous year" as the valuation date in terms of the last day "previous year". [310 G H] The High Courts in India have fixed upon the valuation date, in terms of their last day of a period which is also the relevant period under the Income Tax Act, wealth tax is charged for every assessment year in respect of the net wealth. [310 D] The High courts in India have not fixed upon the first day of the "previous year", as the valuation dates in terms of section 7 as the estimated price, which, in the opinion of the Wealth Tax Officer, the asset might fetch if sold on the valuation dates. [310 E] The High Judges in India have held that accrued tax was liable to levy wealth tax on the basis of the last date of the income Tax Act, and so the reference has been made. [310 H] The question is answered accordingly in favour of Revenue and against assessee. [334 A] The High Judge in India has not followed the decision of the Andhra Pradesh and by the Andhra Pradesh high Court in Commissioner for Wealth Tax, Andhra Pradesh vs Vysya Rao (Orissa). [310 G D] The question of accrued interest is a question of fact and the answer to the question is in the negative.

The petitioner was appointed as a Constable in the Central Administrative Tribunal, New Delhi. He was promoted to the post of Constable in the year 1986. He was placed under suspension by an order dated 27.1.1987. The petitioner challenged the order of suspension before the Central Administrative Tribu nal. The Tribunal rejected the petition on the ground that the petitioner was not a workman within the meaning of Section 2(s) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. The petitioner filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of the Tribunal. The High Court dismissed the writ petition on the view that the petitioner had failed to prove that he was a workman within th e meaning of Section2(s) and that the penalty imposed was too excessive. The petitioner then filed a writ appeal in the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court reversed the order of dismissal on the ground th at the dismissal could be supported on any finding as to substantial misdemeanour for which the punishment could lawfully be imposed, it was not for the Court to consider whether that ground alone would have weigh ed with the authority in imposing the punishment. The Supreme Cour t dismissed the writ appeal on the ground of delay. The Supreme cour t dismissed his writ appeal on t he ground that the Tribunal had no jurisdiction to direct the authority to reconsider th e penalty, for as we have alrea dy observed the order of this Court in State of Orissa vs Bidyabhushan Mohapatra, that the penalty of dismissal from service imposed upon the petitioner was whi msical and ordered his reinstatement in service with fu ll back wages. The Supreme court reversed the order on the ground t hat the penalty of dismissing from service imposed on the petitioner was too excessive and not warranted by the facts and circu m stances of the case. The Supreme Cou rt observed that in the case of proceedings transferr ed to the Tribunal from a civil court or High Court, the Tribu ned had the jurisdiction to consider whether the 33 charge proved alone would have weighed with the authority while imposing the punishment, and if so, what that penalty should be . . A government servant who is aggriev ed by the penalty imposed can agitate in appeal, revision or review as the case may be, that the punishment was too excessive or not warranted by t he facts and circ ustances of the cour tions of the case, the High Court had no jursidiction to direct the authorities to reconsider th at order because in respect of some of the findings but not a ll it appears that there had been violation of the rules of natural justice. The Supreme p etitioner also said (at 227): "The last contention that the penalty was too excessive is not for the court to consider whether t he findings of the Tribunal were relevant or extraneous to the matter. The High Cour t had no jurisdiction if the findings of the Enquiry Officer or the competent authority are based on evidence even if some of it is found to be irrelevant or extraneous to t he matter. If the conclusion of the Inquiry Officer or the Competent Authority is based on evidence, it is not for t he Court to consider t he whether the findings of th e Enquiry Officer or th e competent authority are relevant or extraneous t he matter, and if it is found that there has been violation of th e rules of natural ny, it is for the Court t to consider whether it is justified in imposing the penalty.

Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The question which arose in the suit was whether defendant No. 1 was a tenant in respect of the lands in question should be referred to the Mamlatdar for decision and after his decision is received by the Civil Court if the issue is held against defendant No.2. [727G] 1:7 The jurisdiction is conferred on the Mamlatdar under Section 7 of the Bombay Land Revenue Code. [728G] 1.:8 The jurisdiction is also vested in the Revenue Court under section 8 of the Act, and section 58 of the Act specifically bars the Jurisdiction of all other Courts to settle, decided or deal with the same arising out of any pleadings in this suit. [729G] 1 :9 The jurisdiction is thus vested in the revenue Court under section 58(4) of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act. The jurisdiction is., therefore, vested with the Mamlatdar under the Act and Section 58(2). [758G H] 1.11 The question which arises in the suit is whether defendant No 1 was a trespasser raises a plea of tenancy, a question arises whether his plea of tenancy can be decided by the Civil court as incidental to the grant of relief for possession or is the Civil Court precluded from deciding the same in view of section 8(3) of the the Act. If on the other hand, the Mamlatdar rejects the plea raised under the Tenancy Act, the Civil Court would be entitled to deal with the dispute on the footing that the defendant is a trespasser.

The petitioners were engaged as carpenters in the Wood Working Centre of the Himachal Pradesh State Handicrafts Corporation (the "Corpo ration"). They were paid the minimum wages payable by the Deputy Commissioner for like categories of workmen. The Corporation has adopted the minimum wages prescribed by the Deputy Commis sioner for similar work in the construction industry. The Corporation had adopted the minimum wage payable for similar work. The Corporation, however, adopted the minimum rates payable for similar jobs in the construction Industry. The Corporation adopted the minimum Wages payable for similar works in the construction industries at different parts of the State and no permanent craftsmen are employed. The Corporation was also paying the minimum wages admissible to such employees. The Corporation also adopted the minimum rate payable for similar job in the construction work industry. The Court, therefore, directed the Central Government to fix the pay scale of the petitioners on par with their counterparts in the government service. In the immediate aftermath of the decision in Randhir Singh case, there were bumper cases filed in this Court for enforcement of the right to equality before the law and also to raise the administrative staff in the production centers at different parts o the country and abroad. The Court while rejecting the claim expressed the view (at 100): "But equal pay for equal work is a concomitant of Article 14 of the Constitution. From the averments in the pleadings of the parties it will be clear that the Corporation has no regularly employed carpenters. Unless it is shown that there is a discrimination amongst the same set of employees by the same master in the same establishment, the principle of "equal pay for equal Work" cannot be enforced. Unless it be shown that there are a discrimination amongst tho ities amongst the same sets of employees by th e same master in respect of reliability and responsibility, there may be qualitative difference as regards reliability and responsibility. One cannot deny that often the difference is a matter of degree and that there is an element of value judgment by those who are charged with the administration in fixing the scales of pay and other conditions of service. It is important to emphasize that equal pay for Equal work is a postulate of Article 14. From the pleadings of parties it will also be clear that there is no discrimination amongst the equal pay for equality of opportu nity for all citizens in matters relating to employment or appointment to any office under the State. The Court pointed out that the Corporation had adopted minimum wages payable to carpenters engaged in the construction activity at different parts Of the State and none of the petitioners ' jobs are comparable with the counterparts in Government service. The Court also pointed out that there was a discrimination amongst other similar set of employees. Unless it was shown that there was an element of cost judgment by those in the same cadre on the basis of selection based on merit with due regard to experience and seniority, there may also be qualitative difference in as regards reliability or responsibility. It is also applicable only to skilled and unskilled workers in class IV employees in Government service, the petitioners cannot enforce the right to "equal pay" for equal work". The Court, however, directed the Corporation to apply the rates prescribed under exhibit P. 2 unless the Government makes it applicable to employees of the Corporation. In the instant case, the petitioners are employed by a company incorporated under the . By the general description of their job, one cannot come to the conclusion that every carpenter or craftsmen is equal to the other in the performance of his work. Unless it has been shown that there has been a discrimination amongst th e same set of employee by the same employer, the principle o "equal pay For equal work" cannot be invoked invariably in every kind of service particularly in the area of professional services.

The appellant 's father Sadagopalachar was a minor. He executed a will in favour of his father Sadagamaniachar, and the will was written by the scribe as he dictated the contents of the will. The appellant 's case was that after the death of his father, Sadagopal Goswami became the absolute owner of all the properties and so Lakshmamma was not competent in law to make a will in respect of any of them. The trial court held that the will was not proved to be the last will and testament of Lakshmamma. The High Court further held that the appellant had not established that when Lakshmamma had executed the will she was in a sound and disposing state of mind and that it represented her intentions. The High court further held that even if it had found in favour of the appellant on these two points it would not have been of any help to him because his case must inevitably fail when it is held that the testator fully understood the nature and effect of the dispositions before she put her signature to the will. In this appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the will in question was not proved by the appellant and that the onus was heavy on him to remove the suspicions attending the execution of the will and that the evidence adduced by the appellant was not satisfactory. Held, that the onus of proving the signature of the testatrix on the will was heavy on the appellant to remove the doubtss attending the executing of the will, and since the appellant had failed to prove that the will had been executed by her, the onus was onus on him to prove that Lakshmamma did not really know the contents of her will and put her signature on it when she attested the will. Held, further, that the will did not contain the signature of a testator. The fact that the testatrix had signed the will in one room and Lakshmamma, was not a sufficient indication of the fact that the will signed by the testator. The High Courts were in error in coming to the conclusion that it was not shown that the testatrix fully understood the contents of this will and put his signature on it after the will was executed. The onus was heavy upon the appellant to prove by satisfactory evidence that the will, in question, was signed by her. The onus of proving that the will has been executed by the testator was heavy on his failure to prove that it represented his intentions. The onus, therefore, was heavy on it to prove that there was a will in question before him. The onus had to be considered. The onus to prove the signature of an testator on the will has to be considered in the light of the circumstances of each case. The onus is heavy on the person who signs the will. It is in the light Of these circumstances that the direct evidence about the execution of a will has to been considered. The evidence of the appellant was clearly inconsistent with the appellant 's claim that the testatrix did not at all support the appellant ''s case about previous instructions and so it would be difficult to treat the evidence of this witness as suffi cient to prove that he understood the nature of the recitals before she put his signature to the Will. The evidence adduced by him was clearly inconsistent and inconsistent with the appellants ' case about previous instruction and so it could be safely treated to have known the provisions of the instrument before she put the attesting signature to the document of his own free will. The evidence led by the appellant on the question of the execution of will has to, therefore, be considered.

The appellant company was a dealer in Arc Carbons, manufactured by the appellant company. The appellant company was assessed to sales tax for two assessment years 1965 66 and 1966 77 on the ground that they fall under entry No. 4 of the 1st Schedule of the Andhra Pradesh General Sales Tax Act, 1957, (hereinafter referred to as 'the Act '). The appellant company filed an application for adducing expert evidence to determine the question whether arc carbons manufactured by the company could be covered by the entry under consideration. The Assistant Commissioner of Sales Tax, U.P. Circle, Hyderabad, allowed the application and held that the goods fell within entry 41 of Schedule 1 of the Andhra Nadu General Sales Tax, Act, 1957. The appellant filed an appeal before the Sales Tax Appellate Tribunal, which allowed the appeal and held that they fall within entry 41, Schedule 1 of that Act. The appellant challenged the order of the Sales Tax Tribunal, the High Court held that the entry was not agricultural machinery but was not covered by an entry meant for goods sold for agricultural purposes. The appellant contended that the entry in the schedule was not agricultural goods but was not agricultural. The High Court held, that the entry did not include parts and accessories of motor vehicles. The appellant appealed to this Court. HELD: The entry in the Schedule relates to "motor vehicles" and includes "electrical goods" which are required for use in projectors or other cinematographic equipment. The entry in that schedule does not include parts or accessories of motor vehicle. [696G H] The entry does not include "accessories" which are needed for use in projectsor other cinematographers equipment. [697C] The entry in a schedule is not meant to include parts or accessory of motor vehicles, but excludes certain other articles by putting in the words "not being such articles as are ordinarily used for other purposes than as (1) (1965) 16 S.T.C. (2) (1970) 26 S.T..C. (3) (1970). 26 S. T.C.R. 563 is not intended to include parts of motor vehicles which are required to be taxed indicate that the expression "required for use" has been employed for equipment or accessories connected with the main purpose. The entry is meant to include part of a particular kind of apparatus, would not cease to be covered by that intended entry merely because a purchaser makes some other use of it.

The appellant was the hereditary trustee of the temple. The respondents took a different view and proceeded on the basis that the appellant was a hereditary trustee within the meaning of section 6(9) of the Madras Act 19 of 1951. The Subordinate Judge held that the appellant is a hereditary trustee and the suit was not barred by limitation. The Subordinate judge held that the respondents were hereditary trustees because their office ' devolves by hereditary right or because succession to that office is not hereditary in the sense that on the death of an existing mahant, his chela does not succeed to the office as a matter of course, because the successor acquires a right only 'by appointment and the authority to appoint is vested in the assembly of the bairagis and the worshippets. The Subordinate Court held that the respondent was a hereditary trustees and the suit for setting aside the order of the Subordinate Judge was not barred under section 6(8) of the Act. The Subordinate Judges held that the suit was barred by limitation and the suit filed by the appellant was not barred. The High Court allowed the appeal and set aside the judgment of the Subordinate judge. The appellant appealed to this Court. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The appellant is a mere hereditary trustee within his meaning of section 5(9) and the suit is not barred by Limitation. [446B] The appellant is not a hereditary trustee but is a hereditary office within the meaning Of section 6(7) of the Principal Act. [447C] The appellant was a mere hereditary trustees within the meaning o section 6(6) of the principal Act. The fact of the transmission of the rights, estate, obligations and charges of a deceased person to his heir or heirs does not rest upon independent title, I am inclined to the view that the office of the appellant is hereditary within the meaning ofs. 6(9). [447D] The appellant must be held to be a trustee within the ambit of section 6 (7) of Act 19 of 1950. [448B] The fact of transmission of the right, by which one set of men may, by succeeding another set, acquire a right only by appointment and the Authority to appoint is vest in the assembly. [449C] The fact that the appellant has disposed of the shebaitship in any particular manner and this right of disposition is inherent in the founder or except when usage or custom of a different nature is proved to exist, shebaitship like any other species of heritable property follows the line of inheritance from the founder or even except when usage, custom of a particular nature is proved, shebaitshiplike any other species is proved to exists, shebaitship including even such cases. [445C] The word "succession" in section 6(5) of the Bombay Act 19 of 1954 must be construed along with the phrase "successor" and when so construed that part of the definition would only apply where the ordinary rules of succession under the Hindu law are modified by usage and succession has to be determined in accordance with the modified rules.

The respondents were the heirs and legal representatives of one Amarchand N. Shroff deceased. The Income tax Officer found that the income received by the heirs and the legal representatives after his death was liable to tax under section 24B of the Income tax Act. The Commissioner of Income tax, Bombay City, confirmed the assessment. The respondents preferred an appeal to the Income tax Appellate Tribunal. The Tribunal held that the income which was received by the deceased person before his death was assessable to income tax under section 23B of the Act. The High Court held that the words of sub section (1) of section 24B were not confined to the income received after his death but would have been assessable to income received by him if death had not taken place. The High court held that the Income tax Officer was entitled to assess the total income of the deceased person as if the legal representatives were the assessees and the amount was received by them during the previous year. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the words "or any tax which would have been payable by him under this Act if he had not died" mean that irrespective of the date of receipt of income receivable by a person, if the income is received by his heirs and legal representative after his death, they are liable to pay tax under section24B (1) (b) read with section 24B (1), but in the previous year the income received subsequent to the previous year in which he died. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1) The fiction is limited to the cases provided in the three subsections of section 24 B and cannot be extended beyond the ambit of the liability for the income received in the previous years. [707 B] (2) Where a person dies before the publication of the notice referred to in sub section (2) of section 22 or before he is served with a notice under sub section (3) of section 34, as the case may be, his executor administrator or other legal representative shall, on the serving of the notice under sub sub section (4) of section 23 or section 34, be comply therewith and the Income tax officer may proceed to assess the income received on the amount received by him after his death. [708 C] (3) Where a deceased person is died before the publication, his heirs and the heirs of the deceased are liable to be taxed as income received by them if death had taken place. [709 D] (4) Where a widow received the salary due to her husband before his death but in that previous year she died becomes assessable to income Tax in the relevant assessment year. [710 E] (5) Where a legal representative after her death, but the income received subsequently subsequent to the assessment but in that subsequent year becomes assessable to tax under the Act, the income received thereafter becomes assessable to Income tax in the relevant year. [610 F] (6) Where a Hindu dies before the date of publication of the notification under section 22 or after her death but in the subsequent year, the income is not received by her heirs and legal heirs after their death but in any subsequent year, it is earned by the deceased after his death and to the income earned after his death by his heirs or legal representatives after their death. The Andhra Pradesh Public Employment (Requirement as to Residence) Rules, 1959, were made in pursuance of cl. (1) of article 35 of the Constitution. The petitioners contended that the provisions of the Andhra Pradesh Public Services (Requiresment as to residence in a part of a State, were ultra vires the Constitution. Held, that the provisions in the Andhra Pradesh State Public Employment (Regulation of Employment and Promotion) Rules, 1960, were ultravires the Constitution. It was not necessary to express any opinion whether delegation to the Central and/or State Governments to provide by rules for the further implementing of the law made by Parliament was valid or not. The power is given to Parliament to make any law which prescribes. any requirement as to residence within that State or Union territory prior to appointment, as a condition of employment in the State or Union Territory prior to such appointment, as the case may be, prior to such employment or appointment to an office in that State orUnion territory. The words 'any requirement ' and 'or ' in the First Schedule to the Act, therefore, mean that the requirement of residence in a particular part of the State or the Union territory prior thereto, whether Par liament can delegate this function by making a declaration and leaving the details to be filled in by the rule making power of the Central or State Governments. The words "any requirement as to resident within that State" in the First schedule to the Act mean a requirement as to residential qualification and it is impossible to think that the requirement may be also as to residence outside that State or the State or any particular part of that State or any part of the state. The words in the First and the Second Schedule to the Andhra Pradesh Act, 1957, in so far as it relates to Telengana region will be substituted. The words, 'any requirement as regards residence in a State or Union territories prior to appointment as a condition for residence in a specified State or Union or territory prior to such appointments, ' in so far it relates to ' residence within that Union or territory' are ultra vires the constitution. The words are not intended to give any power to make a law prescribing requirement as to Residence within that State. The words used in the First, Schedule to the Constitution, in so long as it relates, are ultra vires. The words were not intended to convey any such power. The words have been used in the first and the Second Schedules to the Andhra Act, 1957. The words of the First Schedule, in so much as they relate to Telengna region, talauqas, cities, towns or villages. The words cannot be used in the second and the Second schedules to the Andhra State Act, 1957 and the Rules under it are ultra vires and ultra vires the Act. The words must be read as conferring a power to make, a law prescribing a requirement as regards resident within that Union and, therefore, the requirement must be as to residence. The words do not mean that the intention of Parliament was to make a provision for residence in the State and, therefore the requirement must have been understood as conferring a discretion to make, such a law. The words may be used in a particular case and the words must be so construed as to make it a law prescribing. The words should be so construed that it is impossible for Parliament to make a legislation which prescribes. Any requirement as to domicile within a State or a Union territory prior or appointment to a office in that Union or Union territory, any requirement as regards domicile within that State, may be also, as to residence, within that State and, secondly, whether Partiat can delegate this functions by making a declarations and leaving the particulars to be filled by the rule made power of the State Governments.

The appellant was convicted of contempt of court and sentenced to pay a fine of Rs. 1,000/ and further ordered that in case of default they shall undergo simple imprisonment for two weeks. The High Court held that the five appellants had disobeyed an order of stay passed by it staying proceedings pending before the Nyaya Panchayat. The High court held that the Nyaya Panchayat had not taken any steps to comply with the order of stay. The High Curt held that the High Court did not appreciate that the Nyaya Panchayats exercised judicial powers and, even if the Panchas erred in not staying proceedings, before finding them guilty of contempt of Court it should be definitely proved that the order was passed deliberately to by pass the order of the High Court. The High Courts also held that the noncompliance with the order dated December 25, 1963, was not proved. The High "Court also held that there was no evidence to show that the Nyaya panchayat had not taken steps to comply the order of injunction passed by it. The High. Court also held, that the Nyaya panchayats exercised judicial powers, even if they failed to comply with it, the Nyaya Panchayats exercising judicial powers and even if the Panch failed to comply it, the order was not passed deliberately to pass the order. The High Judge also held that it did not appreciate the evidence, but, with respect, it seems to us that the High court did not appreciate this evidence. The HighCourt also held, on examination of the evidence, that it did "not want to rely upon the principles which we have mentioned above, that the order of detention was passed deliberately, to by pass an order of the Magistrate. Contempt of court is a serious matter and a High Court should be chary of finding a judicial officer guilty of contempt. Contempt of Court is a serious matters and a High court should be char y of finding a Judicial officer guilty of Contempt of court for disobeying its orders unless there is unimpeachable evidence that the judicial officer had knowledge of the order of High Court. Contempt of courts is a serious one and a High Courts should be charay of finding ajudicial officer guilty of disobedience of its orders unless it is proved that the judicial Officer had knowledge of that order. Contempt of the court is a grave matter and a high Court should be slow to interfere with the order passed by the High Court." The High Court further held that "it was not proved that any such order was passed intentionally to by pass it the order of a High Court". The High court also held that: "there was nothing in the order sheet to show that it did so. It was not proved by the evidence here that any such applications were made before the Magistrate. The appellant was convicted by the Special Court under section 5(1) of the West Bengal Special Courts Act, to which the appellant was charged, and was sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for a period of six months. The Special Court acquitted the appellant. The appellant filed an appeal to the High Court. The High Court dismissed the appeal. The appellant contended that the classification of the appellant was discriminatory in so far as it authorises the State Government to direct that certain offences or classes of cases should be tried by a special court, the provision was discriminatory and violative of article 14 of the Constitution in so far it authorises the Government to direct "cases" to be tried by special court according to the special procedure prescribed by it for the speedier trial of certain offences. Held, that the classification made by the impugned Act is not discriminatory in so much as it authorises a speedier trials of certain offences; for, it is the State Government which has to select those cases which, in its opinion, require speedier Trial of certain offences and classes of cases, speedier try such offences or classes as, in its judgment, require spei cial court according to its special procedure provided for the spei cedier trial. The classification made by section 5(I) of the Act is not a reasonable classification. The classification is not a classification in the impugned Act as it does not by its own force make the special procedure provided in the Act applicable to the trial of certain cases. The classification of offences or classes or classes of offences or class of cases is, therefore, not a reasonable test. The classification must also be made in the light of the object of the Act as expressed in its preamble, that is to say, the State Government can only select those cases where the procedure laid down in it is to apply, and hence it is necessary to ascertain whether it is actually based on such a classification. It is not the State Government 's notification under the section that attracts the application of the procedure. The classification, therefore, cannot be said to be discriminatory in so long as it authorises speedier d trial of certain offence. The classification cannot be said as it does by its own operation make the special provisions applicable to the trials of certain cases, spei ceting trial of certain classes of offences and classes or classes thereof. The classification can also be made by the State Government in the light o the object of section 5(l) of the , and hence it cannot be said that it is intended to provide for the speetier trial of those offences. The classification may also be made according to the Special procedure provided in section 5(2) of the, Act. The classification in the present case was not a reasonable one. The classification was made by the Government in the exercise of its discretion in the State Government. The classification therefore cannot be said in the absence of any special circumstances which may dis tinguish one offence or one class of offences or one class or classes of persons or cases from another offence, or class of offences, speedien d trial is desirable in the disposal of all offences or classes thereof, speediers trial of certain categories or classes of Cases. The classification thus made by the High Court was not discriminatory in the sense that it was intended to provide that those cases and offences which in the opinion of the State Government would require speedi er trial could be assigned by it to the Special Court. The classification as it does, was not discriminatory. The classification which was made by section 6 of the West West Bengal Special courts Act to be ultra vires the Constitution was not discriminatory and violative article 14 of Constitution.

The petitioner was a registered dealer under the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, and was assessed to income tax for the assessment year 1947 1947 1947 1947. The Income tax Officer rejected the petitioner 's application for registration of the firm under section 5(1) of the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922. The petitioner filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the order of the Income tax Officer. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. The petitioner contended that the provisions of section 5(4) of the Act were void from the date of the commencement of the Constitution by reason of article 14 of the Constitution. Held, that the provisions in section 5(3) of the impugned Act were not void from the very date of the Constitution and that the impugned Act violated article 14 of Constitution. The provisions of section 34 of the Indian Incometax Act, 1922 were not void on the ground that they were inconsistent with the provisions of article 19(1)(g) of the Constitution, and that the provisions were void from that date. The provisions in section 34 of that Act were not intended to operate to the detriment of those dealt with under sub section (4) of section 5 of the Act. The provisions were not intended for the benefit of those dealt under sub section(4) and were intended to operate only to the detriment to those dealt with in sub section (1) of section 34. The provisions contained in section 34 were intended to protect the interests of those dealt in under sub section 4 of section 5 and the provisions of sub section (3) of section 6 were intended to prevent the evasion of tax. The provisions enacted in section 34 are intended to protect those dealt with by sub section (2) of section 4 and the provisions enacted in that section are intended to prevent evasion of tax and to prevent evasion thereof. The provisions are intended to safeguard the interests of the persons dealt with under that sub section. The provisions made in section 34 do not affect the provisions of the Indian Act. The provision enacted in section 5 of that Act are intended to provide a machinery for investigation into escaped income or evaded income. The provisions have been enacted to safeguard the interest of the persons concerned. The provisions relating to escaped income or evasion of tax are intended to secure the interests of persons concerned. It is not intended to protect persons dealt with in subsection (1) and to prevent the imposition of penalty on them. The provisions which are intended to preserve the interests of such persons are intended to be protected against the provisions of sections 34 and 34 of the Act and are intended to achieve the object of the Act, and are intended for protecting the interests of certain persons. The provisions do not affect those dealt with as under sub section 2 of section 34, and those dealt with thereunder. The provisions, therefore, do not affect any of the provisions of any of the sections of the Indian income tax Act and the provisions made in that section. The provision contained in section 5 are intended to serve the purpose of protecting the interests and to prevent avoidance of evasion of tax, and the provisions are intended for the protection of those dealt against under sub section 3 of section 34 and are intended only to protect those dealing with under sub sections (1) to (4) and to protect the persons dealt under under that sub sections. The provisions therefore do not affect section 34 of section 5. The provisions under section 34 are not intended to prevent any person from being prosecuted under that sub sub section. It is intended to protect a person who is being investigated to rebut any evidence brought on the record against him, and that makes all the difference between the two procedures.

The Federation of Indian Chambers of Commerce and Industry, New Delhi, was established under the Delhi Shops and Establishments Act, 1954. The Federation was established under a deed of agreement dated April 1, 1954. Under the terms of the agreement, the Federation was to carry on the business of the Federation. The Federation had to carry on its business in connection with, or incidental or ancillary to trade or business in general within the latter part of the definition. The Federation failed to comply with the direction and contended that it was not an "establishment" as defined in section 2(9) of the Act. The High Court rejected the contention of the Federation and held that it was an "commercial establishment" within the meaning of section 2(5) of the Delhi Shops & Establishments Act, 1958. The Federation preferred an appeal to this Court. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The definition of "commercial establishment " in section 2 (j) of the is far wider than that of "commercial establishments" in section 2. [353D] 2. The definition does not necessarily mean something by which a profit is made. It is immaterial whether its activities bring its premises within the ambit of a "commercial establishment". [353G] 3. The mere word 'trade ' does not necessarily means something by which an profit is made, but it is not distributed among its members. [353G; 353A] 4. The definition is far wider as that of " commercial establishment" in section 3(5) is far wider. [353C] 5. The definition refers to "any particular business or trade carried on in a premises" and is not distributed amongst its members. The fact of the matter is that the activity of the Federation carried on in the premises in question is a business or trade. [353F] 6. The mere words "any work in connection with or incidental or auxiliary to trade or commerce" indicate that the activity carried on by the Federation amounts to a business or profession. [353A] 7. The definition also refers to "some particular business or business in connection therewith or incidental or incidental or allied to trade or trade or business". [353C D] 8. The activity of the Association is not a trade or business. It is not possible to accept the contention that the activity was a trade or trade. The fact that the Federation carried out the activities of the Federation does not necessarily imply something by which the profit is made and is not distribution amongst its members but also the business men and industrialists even if they were not its members. It is true that the definition refers to a particular business or profession but it is immaterial whether it is a trade or a trade. [354C] 9. The mere expression of a trade does not necessarily include something by which any profit is made or. it is not distribution among its members but it is only immaterial whether its activity brings its premises within a wider definition of "industry". [354C D] 10. The fact, of the matter being that the activity in question was a business or business. The fact is that the Federation was systematically assisting not only its members but even if it was not distributed among the members. [354D] 11. The fact was that the activity, of the Federation was a business and trade. The mere fact of the matters is that the activities of a registered society, charitable or other trust will not take it out of the definition if the activity carried out by it amounts to a busi (1)[1971] 1 S.C.R. Mittal 's case (supra) it was held that the activity Of the Federation carried in the premises was a business. [354G] 12.

The assessee was a Hindu undivided family headed by one Sri Trivikram Narain Singh who was a descendant of one Sri Babu Ausan Singh. The Income tax Officer held that it was a regular annual income of the assessee and did not fall within the category of agricultural income tax. The Appellate Tribunal held that it did not fall under the category of Agricultural Income tax. The High Court held that it could not be said that the income arose from a statutory obligation of the Government for extinguishing the proprietary rights of the Jagirdar and when the immediate source of the income was not land or rent collections from land, it was not land within the meaning of section 4(3)(viii) of the Act. The High court further held that the right conferred by the letter dated July 7, 1837, was a right to a share of one fourth in the net land revenue collections after deducting costs of Tahsil establishment. The High ' Court accordingly answered the question in the negative. The Revenue appealed to this Court. HELD: The right conferred by a letter of July 7,1837, was not a right to receive rent or revenue of agricultural lands but rests in the covenant in the deed to receive remuneration for management of the trust. The income of the trust appropriated by the assessee as his remuneration is not received by him as rent or revenue. The income, however, remains the arrangement arrived at in 1837 and, therefore, it is not agricultural income as defined in the Act. [419D] The income of a trust appropriated by a person with whom the land was settled, land revenue is payable by the Government for extinguish the proprietary rights, of the Jagirdar. The income is derived from land within the ambit of the definition in section 2(1)(a) of the Income tax Act, vide C.I.T.v. 36,396/ was chargeable to tax under the Act as the income was never agricultural income for "although the pension was determined with respect to the quantum of the rent collection the rent collections or the land could not be held to be the immediate source for the pension. [421B] The income, therefore, does not acquire the character of an interest in land or in land revenue. [422C] The income is not agricultural Income as defined in section 2 (1)(a). The source of the right in which a fraction of the net income of the Trust is to be appropriated by the appellant as his remuneration, is derived from lands used for agricultural purposes. The income cannot be held to fall within the meaning Of the definition in the Act, and therefore, it was rightly assessed to tax under section 4(4)(viii) [422D] The Income tax Act is a special Act and the income of the trusts appropriated by the Government is not agricultural. [423C] The Income Tax Officer, in spite of the objection of the assessee, held that it is not agriculture income as defined under the Act. He observed that the income of a Trust appropriated by the Income tax Officer as his remuneration was not received by the assessee. The income was not agricultural income within the meaning o the definition in Section 2(1) (a) of Income tax Act. [413D] The amount of Rs. 36,397/ received by the appellant was agricultural income within section 4(2)(viii) and that is so notwithstanding that computation of remuneration is made as a percentage of the income, a substantial part whereof is derived from the lands used for agriculture purposes. [424B] The Income ' tax Officer, in view of the fact that the income was received by the respondent as his remuneration and not by the assessee, the income was rightly assessed.

The appellant State Transport Undertaking, filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the provisions of Chapters IV and IV A of the Act. The High Court held that the State Transport Undertaking was not entitled to preference in the matter of stage carriage permit. The State Transport Undertaking filed a writ appeal in this Court. The High court held that the proviso to section 63(7) did not offend article 14 of the Constitution. The State Government filed a writ application in the High court challenging the validity and correctness of the order of the High Court. The State of Karnataka filed a writ in the High Courts challenging the validity. The High Courts held that the fourth sub clause of the proviso to sec. 63(7), did not offend Article 14 of the constitution. The High ' Court held that in the back ground of the provisions contained in sections 49, 50, 51, 57, 58, 59 A, 60, 61 and 64 the State Transport Undertakings were not entitled to the preference. The State 's appeal to this Court was dismissed. In the appeals to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court and the State Transport Appellate Tribunal were wrong in distinguishing the decision of this Court in Sher Singh 's case and that the fourth proviso to section 64(7) was unconstitutional and violative of article 14 of Constitution. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The proviso to section 66(7) does not say that in the case of inter State route, the Undertaking will have preference in the matters of stage carriage permits. [1015 E] 2. The proviso does not say for example, like section 68 F(1) that the permit shall be granted to the State Transport undertaking. [1016 F] 3. The proviso provides that in the cases of inter State routes, the claims of all eligible applicants must be considered on merits, applying the rules of preference wherever the claims are approximately equal. [1017 F] 4. The proviso is unconstitutional and it is not violative of article14 of the Constitution, as it is violative of article 19 of the Constitution and so to interpret the word 'preference ' occurring in section 47(1) of the Act, under the former of which the State Transport undertakings would have preference whereas under the latter the State Transport Authority would have preference in preference to be given under section 47(7). [1015 F] 5. The proviso cannot be read as a whole and so to construe the word 'Preference ' occurring therein. [1018 F] 6. The proviso, therefore, does not say, for example, that in the matter o grant of permits from the Indian Tourism Development Corporation, the Undertaking would have preference In the matter of Stage Carriage permit.

The respondent purchased a business in the name of a dealer as defined in the Madras General Sales Tax Act, 1939 (Madras Act No. IX of 1939) from the appellant. The appellant purchased the business in the year of account. The respondent claimed that the appellant was liable to pay sales tax due from the dealer in respect of the sales of which took place before the transfer of the business under Rule 21 A of the Rules framed in exercise of the powers conferred on the State Government by section 19(1) of the Act. The appellant contended that the respondent was not liable to pay the sales tax due by the appellant on the sale of the business. The Sales Tax Officer rejected the claim. The appellant appealed to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner rejected the claim and held that the appellant had no authority under the Act to create a legal fiction by which the transferee of the business was constituted as the dealer liable to pay tax in respect of his turnover. The appellant then appealed to the Sales Tax Tribunal. The Tribunal held that the respondent had no authority to create a statutory fiction by which it could create a legal deeming fiction by which a transferee of the property is constituted as the purchaser liable to pay such tax. The Tribunal also held that the sale of a business was not a sale within the meaning of section 2(1) (c) of the Madras General sales Tax Act, 1948. The Tribunal, however, held that the sales of the business were not sales within the meaning Of section 2(2)(c) of that Act. The Tribunal further held that the purchase of the business in question was not a sales within the definition of the Act and that the sale was not a purchase within the meaning section 2(3)(c) and that the sales were not sales in the sense of the term 'sale ' in section 2(4)(c) Of the Act. On appeal by the appellant, the High Court held that the transaction was not a 'sale within the meaning ofs. 2(3) (c). The High Court held, that the sale in question was a sale within section 2(a) of the, Madras General Sales tax Act, 1939 and that the appellant could be made liable for arrears of sales tax due on the sale. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the respondent undertook to pay the arrears of sales Tax due by the transferor to the transferor, it did not follow 66 that there was a liability created inter se between the State Government on the one hand and the transferee on the other hand. Held, that the respondent did not commit any default in paying according to the notice of assessment, the whole of the amount outstanding on the date of default was charged on the property of the person liable to pay it. The respondent undertook to make payment according to the notices of assessment, not being less than fifteen days from the date of service of the notice. The respondent did not pay according to the intimation of assessment, and the amending Act had no application.

The plaintiff was a public servant and was employed in the State of Gujarat. He was dismissed from service on February 2/4, 1955. The plaintiff filed a suit for a declaration that the order of dismissal was illegal and void on the ground that it contravened the provisions of article 311(2) of the Constitution. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court held that there had been a breach of article 311 of the Constitution and that the liability for the payment of arrears of pay was the liability of the State of Maharashtra and that the plaintiff was not entitled to any relief. The State of Bombay appealed to this Court. HELD : (1) The words,actionable wrong other than breach of contract ' in this context are wide words and include something more than torts, but even so where a suit is brought by a Government servant for arrears of salary, the decree more properly falls under section 60 of the Act rather than under section 61. [179 G] (2) The words ,actionable wrong others than breach of contracts ' in this case are wide words. The case (Reilly vs R.) (2) shows that there may be contractual rights existing before determination of a contract at will which are not inconsistent with a power to determine. [179 E] (3) The case (reilly vs R..) (2), shows that there might be contractual rights between a public servant or Government and are based on contract within the meaning of section 60 of that Act rather than a breach of contract. [179 F] (4) The case of arrears of salary earned by a public servant for the period that he was actually in office. The liability to pay arrears of salary is a liability in respect of an actionable wrong other than a breach in contract. [180 G] (5) The liability to make payment of arrears by a public Servant for the period during which he has served. [180 C] (6) The liability for the pay of arrears of wages earned by a private servant for the time during which he had served. [182 D] (7) The liability arising out of a contract within the ambit of section 60 is a liability arising out a contract within section 60 of Bombay Reorganisation Act, 1960. [180 D] (8) The liability of the Government is a liability which arises out of a breach of a contract. The plaintiffs ' land lies immediately to the south of the defendants ' land. The plaintiffs alleged that the defendants had encroached upon their coal mines on the southern side and removed coal from the encroached portion and had rendered the remaining coal of the encroached portion unworkable. The plaintiffs further alleged that the suit was not barred by limitation and that they would be entitled to the reliefs prayed for. The defendants ' predecessor in interest, denied the allegation and stated that the plaintiffs had encroached upon the plaintiff ' coal land, that the suit had been filed within three years of the date of the filing of the suit. The defendants denied the allegation that the plaintiffs were bound to keep a barrier of 25 feet to the south and removed coal left by the plaintiff in the encroached area. The defendants did not deny the fact that the plaintiffs ' and the defendants had knowledge of the sinking of the quarries and pits in the encroached land. The defendants also did not deny that the plaintiffs' land was entirely lost to them by being rendered unworkable. The defendants pleaded that the suit should be dismissed. The trial court held that the defendants were bound to maintain a barrier of 50 feet to the north of the defendant 's working and, therefore, the coal that was left in the encroached portion was not by any means accessible to the plaintiffs and being thus wholly unworkable was entirely lost. The High Court held that the plaintiffs are bound to keep an barrier of 25 ft to the south. The High court accepted the finding of fact arrived at by the courts below that the initial burden of proof was on the defendants to prove that they had knowledge of that encroachment only within three years thereof. The High ' Court held that in 1932 there was a survey of the plaintiffs ' leasehold and the defendants ' coal that was still left in the encroachment area was entirely lost by being rendered impracticable. The High Curt held that the initial onus of proof was upon the defendants to establish that they had known the sinking of their quarries and pits within three years from the date of filing of the plaint. The High "Court further held that the onus of proof to prove knowledge on the part of the defendants beyond the prescribed time was on the respondents to prove that the initial duty of proof was not on the defendants. The HighCourt held that the burden of proof to establish knowledge on the defendant was on the appellant, and that the initial obligation of proof was discharged. The High Courts held that the finding of the High Court that the initial of burden was on the appellants was contrary to the tenor of the article in the Limitation Act and also to the rules of evidence. The High courts held that the decision of the High court that the initial heavy burden was on them was erroneous. The High appeals by certificate were filed by the defendants. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The High. Court arrived at the finding of facts on the assumption that the initial initial burden was on respondents to prove the knowledge of the defendant within three years, of the date when they had knowledge that the entire burden was on him. [723C] 2. The High curt held that in 1931 there was a Survey of the plaintiffs' and defendants ' coal, the coal was left in their encroached area was entirely loses to them by having been rendered unworkable. [724D] 3. The High, Court, in the cross examination, accepted the finding. The High Judge accepted the finding that the initial evidence was on the record. The High Count held that the first burden was on defendants ' coal and the second burden was on plaintiffs ' coal that is still left in their possession. The High CCurt held that there was no acceptable evidence on their part to establish that the initial was on the defendant ''s possession of the converted property and that the entire onus was on the plaintiff.

The appellant was a crosscutter. He was caught hold of by other workmen and taken outside. On June 25, 1958 Sankaran was informed that the proposed inquiry, if conducted, would lead to further friction and deterioration in the rank and file of the employees in general and also that maintenance of discipline in the undertaking would be prejudiced if he was retained in the service of the appellant and for which a departmental inquiry was intended to be held and he was also placed under suspension pending inquiry. On July 8, 1958 Sankaran, was informed that in view of his denial, a departmental inquiry would be held and it was also a colourable exercise of the power conferred. On July 9, 1958 Sankaran came drunk to the mill and abused the Engineer, the Secretary and others and threatened them with physical violence. The appellant was caught hold by other workmen. The tribunal held that the action taken under r. 18(a) of the Standing Orders was bona fide and was not a bona fide exercise of the powers conferred. The tribunal also held that the appellant had intended to take disciplinary action against the workman but subsequently departmental proceedings were dropped and action was taken under r 18(a). The appellant challenged the order of the tribunal before the High Court. The High Court held that the order terminating the services of Sankaran under r.18(a) was a colourable exercise and that the action was taken in accordance with r. 18 (a) of Standing Orders which is a term of contract between the appellant and its employees to dispense with the service of any employee at any time by just giving 14 days notice or paying 12 days wages. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The appellant failed to satisfy the tribunal when the matter came before it for adjudication that the exercise of the discretion in this case was bona fide. [18C] 2. The appellant did not satisfy the tribunal while the matter came to before it for determination that the exercise was bona fide or was a result of victimisation or unfair labour practice it would have jurisdiction to intervene and set aside such termination. [18D] 3. The appellant had not made any attempt to defend the action taken against Sankaran. [18E] 4. The appellant could not satisfy the Tribunal when the matter was before it for decision that the exercise under r. 19(a) by leading evidence before the tribunal to show that there was in fact misconduct and therefore the action taken was under r. 12. [18F] 5. The appellant has failed to satisfy that the exercise Of the power in this case is bona fide and is not a colourable exercise. [18G] 6. The appellant cannot be accepted at its face value. [18H] 7. The appellant is not entitled under r. 17(a) to the facts of this case because the employer wanted to take action for misconduct actually charged might be done away with. [18B] 8. The appellant, in the present case, was not justified in contending that it is entitled under r 18 (a), of the Standing Order which is a terms of contract between its employees to dispensing with the service and for which an inquiry was intended. [18A] 9. The appellant also failed to satisfy us when the matter coming before it for consideration that the exercise is bona fide or is not colourable exercise of power and that it is now well settled that if the employer wanted a departmental inquiry which was intended to take action under r. 9, there was nothing for it to justify before the tribunal. [18 B] 10. The appellant fails to satisfy the Tribunal that there was a in fact misconduct or unfair labour practices it would have the jurisdiction to intervene or set aside such an termination. [19A] 11.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 Indian Penal Code and sentenced to suffer imprisonment for life. The High Court acquitted the appellant. The appellant preferred an appeal to this Court. The appellant contended that the discrepancies in the evidence of P. 1 to 3 were of a minor character and that the discrepancies noticed by the learned Sessions Judge were of a major character and that they have been unduly magnified by the learned Judges. W. 1 to3, which was supported by the evidence and the accused were entitled to the benefits of doubt. The High court was well justified. The fact that a Parliament did not enacting any other law, even then for th e investigation into allegations o f corruption against a subordinate Judge and for his trial and punishment for that offence, and rest content simply with enacting the, to provide for tile procedure for removi al of a judge under Article 124, clauses (4) and 5 of the Constitution, cannot obviously be applied to the Judges o f India, since the incumbent of the office of Chief Justice of the High court Judges, much greater the Supreme Court judges: The incumbent of the Office of Chief Justice, exercising only moral authority, over his colleagues, in the Supreme court and the High court judges, which has no judicial sanction behind it makes it justiciable. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income tax Officer. The Appellate Tribunal held that the income of the appellant was not taxable as income under section 10. The High Court held that the appellant was entitled to set off the loss incurred in British India business in the former Travancore State of Travancore, and the losses under the head business were sustained in an Indian State and exempt from tax under the Travancore Income tax Act. The appellant contended that the business profits and gains of the business were not taxable as business losses incurred by him in British India or business in British India. Held, that the business in the Travancore State of Cochin was not taxable in the Travancore Act, and the appellant was rightly entitled to set of the loss incurred under the head " business " in the former Cochin State. The appellant was entitled under the Travancore law to set off loss of profits and gains arising under the head ' business in the two territories, i. e., British India and the losses arising under the heads mentioned in section 3 or the provisions of clause (e) of sub section (2) of section 14. The mere use of the words loss of profits or gains to be, set off against profits and gains would not be sufficient to restrict the scope of the proviso to the profits and losses arising under those heads. The mere fact that the word " income " is not used does not justify the construction. that the intention of the Legislature was to restrict the set off of profits and losses to the profits or gains arising under one head against income, profits or gains under another head. The mere absence of any positive words which would support an interpretation in favour of the disintegration of the head " ' and compel the application of the proviso, does not lead to the conclusion that the intention was to restrict set off loss under the head, business in the three territories, i e., British Indian and the Indian States. The mere mere use of words loss of profit or loss to be, sets off against profits or gains from business or to modify the mode of computation under section 10, and not under section 24(1) (Per Bose, J.) (1) [1946] A.C.R. 969. (2) 269 argument does not take note of the definition of total income under section 3 or section 4 where in the case of a resident 'total income ' includes income, profits and gains accruing or arising to him within or without British India or Indian State and would under the provisions of section 4, have been exempted from tax. The mere mention of the word "income " in the proviso does not justify this construction. The mere existence of the words " loss of profits" does not justify that the construction. was to restrict setting off loss of profit and losses arising in Indian States only to business or to alter the mode of calculation under section 10 and not to modify the method of computation under sections 10 and 12B and not to any other section. The mere possession of the words ' loss of profits to be, and not the use of the word ' income ' does not justify, the construction. The use of the expression " loss of profit" does not support the construction. That is done under section 10 or section 12B and cannot be sufficient to limit the scope of section 10.

[448 D] 1.6 The Tribunal had wrongly taken into account that in all those awards in recent time in various concerns the trend had was to fix retirement ages at 58. 430 The very few departedures from this procedure which the Tribunal had mentioned are, In our opinion, the Tribunal had not correctly appreciated the fact and circumstances disclosed and the fact that it was not correct to say that it was in fact incorrect to say that what was observed by itself on the earlier occasion and were confirmed by this court in appeal, is on the whole sound. The respondent no. 2, the owner of a Five Star Hotel, filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the lease. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The land allotted to respondent No. 3 was a Garden hotel and there was no chance of the ecology and environment improving as a result of planting numerous trees all around the proposed hotel and the removal of the burial ground and dumping ground for rubbish. [623C] 1.2 The State was giving tapping contract simpliciter there can be no doubt that the State would have to auction or invite tenders for securing the highest price, subject, of course, to any other relevant overriding considerations of public interest. But in a case like this where the State is allo cating resources such as water, power raw materials etc. for the purpose o encouraging setting up industries within the state and invite those interested to come up with pro posals for the purpose. [624E] 1.3 The State would have been justified in proceeding on the basis that the State had made available to this Court all documents in connection with the proposal for lending over a piece of the State Government land to respondent No.. 3. [625B] 1.4 The State was given tapping contract simplicitor there can be an infinite variety of con siderations which may have to be taken into account by the Government in formulating its policies and it is on a total evaluation of various considerations which have weighed with the Government in taking a particular action, that the Court would have to decide whether the action of the Government is reasonable and in public interest. [626C] 1:5 The State was not bound to advertise and tell the people that it wants a particular industry to be set up within the State and invite those participating to come up With pro posals to for the purpose, that the court would have to judge whether the action is reasonable and it is in public interest that the Court will have to decide if the action of Government is reasonable. Bearing in mind the proper approach that we have to make when 263 questions of ecology and environment are raised, an approach which we have mentioned at the outset, we are satisfied that the State was giving opportunity to this Court to decide whether it wants a specific industry to be Set up within the state. The yardstick of price in the open market would be wholly inept, because in view of the State Policy, there would be no question of any resin being sold in the openmarket. The appellant, a co sharer, was a tenant in the suit land. The vendor was a co sharers. The vendor had purchased the suit land from the vendor. The vendor sold the suit land to the appellant. The appellant filed a suit for pre emption. The suit was decreed by the trial court. The appellant challenged the decree of the trial court in a suit for preemption. The trial court dismissed the suit. The appellant preferred an appeal before the High Court. The High Court dismissed the appeal. The High court held that the suit land belonged to more than one co sharer and had not been sold jointly by all the co sharers jointly. The High, Court held that the right of pre emption conferred on the vendor by section 15(1)(a) of the Punjab Preemption Act, 1913 was a reasonable restriction on the right to hold, acquire or dispose of property conferred by Article 19(1)(f) of the Constitution. The High ' Court, however, did not find any justification for the classification contained m section 15(2) of the Act. The High "Court further held that the interpretation placed by the two judge Bench on the expression 'other co sharers ' in section 15(I)(b) of the said Act was not correct. The HighCourt further held, that the interpretation put by the two Judge Bench on the expressions 'other cosharers ' in section15(1)(b) and clause fourthly of section 15( 1)(c) was not correct and that the interpretation placing the expression 'Other co sharers' in the fourth clause was not correct, and that the effect of the amendment was that the effect was to deny the right of the pre emption to those relatives or relatives of the vendor or vendors who were specified in the erstwhile first three clauses of section 15 (1)(b). The High Court also held that the view taken by the two judges on the expression "other co sharer ' in section 14(1)(c) of the Haryana Preemption Act was not proper. The High Curt held that the amendment made in 1960 provided that where the sale is of a share out of joint land or property and is not by all the cos sharers jointly, only the other co sharers and the tenants can exercise the right of preemption under clause 'fourthly ' and with a view to covering all the remaining co sharers not specifically mentioned the preceding clauses it used the expression 'any co sharer is left out. The appellant was an Advocate of the High Court of Bombay. He was a standing of about thirty years. The grounds were not vague or not. The grounds furnished were vague. The alleged vagueness of the grounds furnished and the alleged unsustainable claim for non disclosure under article 22(6) of the Constitution on behalf of the detaining authority, to get over the alleged vagueness. The High Court dismissed the application. The appellant appealed to this Court. The appellant contended that the grounds furnished were not vague and not vague. Held, that the grounds were vague and not not vague. The right of the detenue to be furnished particulars, at least to that extent, it will enable him to present to the Advisory Board his difficulties in making a proper representation and to convey to it a request for obtaining the requisite particulars from the State under section 10 of the Act for their own information and consideration. The right to be furnished the particulars, at the time, from the detaining authority to the State under article 22 (6) of Constitution cannot be so exercised as to nullify the constitutional right of the petitioner for being afforded a proper opportunity of representation. The right cannot be so construed as to nullify or destroy the constitutional right to be afforded a proper hearing. The right is subject to the limitation under article 22 of the Constitution. The right can be so exercised if the petitioner has exercised his right to ask for particulars at the time when the grounds were furnished. The right has to be imputed in a case where no particulars are at all furnished. The power not to disclose facts considered against public interest cannot be so exercise as to nullify a constitutional right of representation. Such a contention as to the mala fide exercise of the power is untenable in the present case having regard to the nature of the 393 grounds on which the detention is based and the nature of activities imputed to the appellant. The right, therefore, cannot be so interpreted as to nullify its constitutional right of being afforded a reasonable opportunity of representation and an obligation to communicate cannot be implied in these circumstances. The right conferred on the detenue to make a representation is subject to a limitation under article 19(6) whereby disclosure of facts considered to be against public interest. The right may be so exercised, as to nullify that constitutional right cannot be said to be subject to the limitations under article 22. The right under article 22 cannot be so regarded as to nullify constitutional right of a detenue for being afforded an adequate opportunity of representation, and an obligation has to be shown to have been imposed on the detaining authority. The right must be shown to be founded on a consideration of the circumstances of each case, as was pointed out by this Court in the State of Bombay vs Atma Ram Sridhar Vaidya(1) in the following passage: "The right to be supplied particulars, at a time it was in public interest to disclose the details referred to in the particular paragraph of the affidavit and there is nothing to suggest that this question was not considered by the detaining authority at the time of the grounds being furnished. The non communication of the decision cannot be held to have hampered his constitutional right of making a proper request and an obligation on the part of the detaining Authority to communicate cannot, therefore, be implied in this regard."

The appellant No. 1 was prosecuted under section 31(1) read with section 33(1) of the Act and sentenced to a fine of Rs. 5 to a fine. The appellant No. I was acquitted by the Chief Presidency Magistrate. The appellant Nos. 1 and 5 were convicted and the others were acquitted. The High Court reversed the order of acquittal and convicted the appellant No. 5 under section 31 of the Act. The High court held that as the conciliation proceedings had continued for a period of more than 14 days as from January 17, 1952, further proceedings for conciliation were illegal and therefore the appellant No, 5 could not be convicted under section 31 (1) of The Act. Held, that the conciliation proceedings were not pending when Louis Pereira was dismissed. Section 12(6) of the , is not an offence punishable with imprisonment for a period which may extend to six months or with fine or with both. The words " pendency of conciliation proceedings" in section 12(6), are not intended to refer to the dispute as the termination of the conciliation proceedings is deemed to take place when the report of the Conciliation Officer is received by the appropriate Government or when the report is received by that Government. The words ' pendency of conciliation proceeding' in section 12 are not intended merely to refer to a dispute as the dispute is arrived at when the report under section 12( 6) is made by the Conciliation Officer. The words are not intended only to refer to an industrial dispute as the conciliation proceeding is pending. The words used in section 12 (6) are not intended for the purpose of giving effect to the provisions of the Act but they are intended to refer only to the dispute which is referred to the conciliation officer or a Board or of any proceeding before a Labour Court or Tribunal or National Tribunal. The words in section 12 of the Act are intended to give effect to the intention of the legislature. The words of section 12(5) are intended to convey the intention of Parliament to give effect and to the intention that the conciliation proceeding should be held to terminate when the report received by the Conciliation officer is received by him. The words cannot be construed to mean that the legislature intended that the conciliation should be held in the case where no settlement is arrived at, when the report was received by the Appropriate Government or when that report is received within 14 days of the commencement of the conciliation proceeding. The words must be construed to include the words ' pendency in conciliation proceedings '. The words should be construed to refer to proceedings closed within a fortnight and if for some reason the Conciliation Officer delays the submission of his report his action (1) ; No doubt section 12 contemplates that the report should be made and the proceedings closed within one week and if proceedings are not closed but are carried on, as they were in the present case, or if the Conciliation Officer does not make his report within 14 days he may be guilty of a breach of duty but in law the proceedings do not automatically come to an end after 14 days but only terminate as provided in section 20(2)(b) of the act. The words, ' pendency in the conciliation proceedings ' in section 12, are intended to indicate that the conciliation is to be held in a particular case where no settlements are arrived at, where no settlement was arrived at, while the report under s. 12(6)(b) is made.

The appellants were the owners of a notified commercial crop in the State of Madras. The appellants were the sellers of the notified commercial crops in the State. The appellants filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the bye law. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. The appellants contended that the appellants were not prevented from doing their business, for they could still utilise it for commodities other than the notified crops. Held, that the appellants have really two fundamental rights: one is to carry on trade or business and the other is to hold their property, i.e., the market; that by reason of the notification they are not prevented from carrying on their business, and that they are not prohibited from holding the market as property, for they can still utilise it towards commodities other than those notified crops. The question whether the allowance is permitted to be received by the rules or bye laws framed thereunder, as section 14 prohibits the deduction of trade allowance and does not operate upon any other payments made which are not trade allowances, is a trade allowance and if so, whether the allowance was permitted to be receive by the rules and bye laws made under that section. The question should be answered in favour of the appellants.
