The petitioner was appointed as officiating Executive Engineer in Class I service in the Central Public Works Department under the Ministry of Works and Housing of Government of India and was compulsorily retired by order dated 3.7.1976 with effect from 5.11.1976. The petitioner was compulsorily retired from service on the date of the order. The petitioner challenged the order for retirement and has claimed payment of remuneration which he would have been entitled to draw upto the normal date of superannuation. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that the petitioner was not in Class I or Class II service or post and that he was not entitled to salary and other service allowances payable to him from the date of compulsory retirement. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The petitioner had not attained the age of 50 years by the date of his order. The possibility of a reversion to the substantive post is not germane to the exercise of power contained in F.R. 56(j)(i) after he has attained the age Of 50 years. [608G H] 2. The purpose of Fundamental Rules 56(j) is to confer power on the appropriate authority to compulsorily retire Government servant in the public interest and the classification of Government servants into two categories, namely, (i) the Government servant is in Class I and Class II service; (ii) in any other case after he has completed the age of 55 years after he has had attained the ageof 50 years; and (iii) in any case after he had attained the said age of fifty five years. The possibility that a person who is in Class II service and is therefore, a temporary hand, he has no right to the post and is therefore liable to be reverted to the post, if any, on which he has a lien. [609B] 3. The purpose behind the sub clauses is to confer powers on the appropriate authorities to compulsorily retire government servants in the public interests and the classification is to classify Government servants into three categories, namely (i) Government servant officiating in Class I, Class II service, or post, (ii) who at the relevant time was in Class I Service or post, whether substantively, temporarily or on officiating basis. [610C] 4. The purpose for the sub clauses (i) and (ii) has a purpose behind it. If the condi tion indicated in sub clause (i) is satisfied, namely the Government servant was in Class II or Class II Service or post at the relevant point o f time and he had attained th e age of fifty, the further condition that he must substantively belong to the two classes of service or post, either substantively, temporarily, temporarily oron officiating basis. If the officia tion is not brought to an end by reverting the Government servant to his substantive post before the power of compul sory retirement is exercised, the Government servant con cerned must be taken to be in Class Ior Class II service. [611B] 5. The possibility is of a reversion from the substantive post being held on substantive basis. If a Government servant is only a temporary hand he has no rights to the post but can be reverted to his substantive position before the power is exercised, if any. The possibility cannot be introduced into the scheme. If the pers sion indicated in sub clauses (ii) is satisfied , namely the Government Servant is in Class 1 or Class II services or post, he has a right to the posts and can always be reverted to that post, if anyone has to go back to the substantive posts, if any on which he had a lien. The possibility o f a reversion to a substantive post is also not germane to a exercise of power under sub clause (ii).

The trial court dismissed the suit. The High Court held that the order of the High Court was a final order within the meaning of article 133 (1) (c) since the controversy between the parties when the complaint in respect of offences under sections 467 and 468 read with section 114 I.P. Code was concerned merely with an order passed by the High Court which maintained the order of Additional Sessions Judge that a complaint under section 205 read with section 109 I.P., Code could be filed against the appellant. The High court held that the expression "final order" in article 133 ( 1) (c ) since the controversy was decided, and the trial court decided the issue against the appellant and the order was confirmed in appeal by the High court. The appellant company then filed a petition for winding up of a company as to the maintainability of a claim for recovery of income tax dues. The High, Court held that an order passed in a petition for setting aside an order of the Additional Sessions Judge was a final one within the meaning Of article 133 (I) (c), since the controversy involved was merely with an application for winding up, the order was not final. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The expression "final" in article133 (1) of the Constitution means a final adjudication by the Court of the rights of the parties in dispute in a suit or proceeding. If the decision on an issue put an end to the suit, the order is not final. [419D] 1.2 The expression "judgment" in article 134(1) (C) of the constitution means a final order, as far as this Court is concerned merely with a order passed by a High Court which maintaining the order of a High Court, and does not include the order deciding an important point or even a vital issue in the case. If the order deciding the issue put an d end to the trial, the order will undoubtedly be a final one, but if the suit is still left alive and has got to be tried in the ordinary way, no finality could attach to the order. [420E] 1.3 The expression "decree" in article 136(1) of Civil Procedure means a final decision on the rights of parties in dispute. If the judgment on an issue puts an end to a suit, the suit or proceeding from which appeal has arisen, the order becomes interlocutory. [421B] 1.4 The expression "order" in article 137(1) means a final determination by the Court. If the Court does not, and the suit or proceedings is a live one, yet to be tried, the order would undoubtedly be afinal one, but, if after the order is made, the suit is not still left alive. [422C] 1.5 The expression "interlocutory order" in Article 136(1)(c) means a decision which finally determines the rights and liabilities of the parties.

The appellant was appointed as a clerk on June 1, 1963 by the Panchayat Samiti, Loharu, which is respondent 3 in this appeal. The appellant was appointed on June 1. 1975 by the Panchayat Samitis, Loharo, which is respondents 3 in this case. On March 14, 1975, the appellant was appointed to the post of a Head Clerk on an ad hoc basis in January 1974. On March 13, 1975, a resolution was passed by the Panchayat Parishad, Lohawru, which was respondent 3 in the appeal. The resolution was passed on April 1, 1975, by the Panchayat Raj Samiti, Lohru, which, according to the terms and conditions of his service with the Panchayat Samiti was published in the Haryana Gazette on June 13, 1973. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court of Punjab and Haryana, asking that he should be absorbed as a Head Clerk in any event. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the appellant was entitled to continue in the service of the Panchayat on the same terms and conditions on which he was employed by the Panchayat. The appellant challenged the validity of the resolution on the ground that the appellant had not been appointed as a Head clerk on April 1. 1975, being the date on which the Panchayat Samiti lost its power to make appointments to the Panchayat Samiti until he was absorbed in Government service. The appellant contended that the appellant could not be absorbed as Head Clerk on April 1 1975 on a regular basis in January 1975 on a post in which the Panchayat Samitis were divested of their power to make appointment to the Panchayat Samitis until he was appointed validly in the post of Head Clerk on June 13. 1973. The High court dismissed the writ application holding that the right to be considered for promotion is a term and condition of service, and that the appellant is entitled to continue as a Head Cashier on the same conditions on which the he was employed. The appellant, therefore, filed this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The right to be consider for promotion is an term and condition. The right to consider for promotion, is a term, and condition of Service, what is relevant for our purpose is not whether the appellant was entitle to be considered to be promoted but, whether the Panchayat Samiti had the right to appoint him to the post. [723B] 1.2 The right to appoint a Head Clerk is a term or condition of service. What is relevant for the purpose is not Whether the appellant was right to be treated for promotion but, whether he was entitled to be considered as a Head Accountant on the date on Which it purported to do. [724C] 1.3 The right to appointment is a term. [725B] 1:4 The right to the post is a term but condition of service and what is relevant is not whether it has been acquired by the Panchayat or by the Panchayat, and that is the post in which it purported to act. [726C] 1:5 The appointment of the appellant to the post was made after June 13,1973 when the Amending Act came into force. [727C] 1.:6 The appellant was entitled, to be considered in the post on which he had been appointed validly in accordance with the terms and condition of his service.

The appellants were displaced persons from West Pakistan. They were allotted quasi permanent allotment of 24 standard acres and 15 3/4 units in the village of Raikot in Ludhiana District in 1949. The Custodian General for the State of Punjab recommended to the Custodian General the restoration 331 of the land to the 14 allottees which had been taken away from them by reason of cancellation of the allotment in their favour by the order dated October 31, 1952. The appellants ' application was rejected by the Deputy Custodian General on the ground that his jurisdiction to revise the order had been taken off by virtue of the provisions of , (44 of 1954) and the notification issued thereunder on March 24, 1955, and the notification dated March 24,1955, was published in the official Gazette of that State dated March 24 1955, and such property was acquired under the provisions of the , (44) of 1954) as the property vested in the Central Government. The appellants filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the notification and the notification. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. The appellants contended that the power of the Custodian under the , to revise the orders has been taken away by virtue of section 10 of the Act and the notification published thereunder on March 9, 1955, was published on March 24 1955 and published in the Official Gazette of that Government dated March 24. 1955, and that the notification issued under section 12(1) of the Act was published in that Gazette on March 24.1955, and that therefore the notification issued by the Central Government under section 12 of the Act on March 24 was void. Held, that the power to revise the allotment of any property to a person or to cancel an allotment or lease made in favour of a person rests on the fact that the property vests in him. The power of the Central Government to revise the decision of the Custodian is in conflict with section 10 of Act and the rules made thereunder. The power to revise its order has been conferred by section 19 of the Act. The power under section 19 of Act is not completely in conflict with the section 10 of that Act. The Custodian, by reason of the divesting of the property, as from March 24, 1954, had become functus officio with respect to it and could not rectify any error made by him in the past in the matter of cancellation of allotment. Sub section (2) provides that subject to the provisions of section 10, a managing officer or a managing corporation may, among other things, take such measures as he or it considers it necessary or expedient for the purpose of securing, administering, preserving, managing or disposing of any property in the compensation pool entrusted to him or it. etc. etc. The consequence of the publication of the notification by the Central government under section 12 (1) of this Act continues to be evacuee property. The consequence is that the property, though vested in the Custodian, by virtue of sub section (2), continues to be an evacuee property. [7H] The power of a managing officer to cancel an order passed under section 12 is in conflict With section 10 of this Act. The consequence would be to divest the Custodian completely of his right in the property flowing from section 8 of the , and vest that property in the Central government. Sub section 2 provides that subject, to the provisions Of the Act and rules made thereunder, a managing committee or a managing committee may, among others, take such steps as he or they considers it necessary for the purpose for securing, administering , preserving, managing, disposing of any properties in the compensation Pool entrusted to him, or it. The consequence, of the publication by the Central Govt under section 12, of the with respect to any property or a class of property would be to deprive the Custodian completely Of his right in property flowing from the section.

The appellant, a mahant of the Dera, was appointed mahant of Dera at Landeke. The defendant, died on 13 10 1970. The appellant, who was the lawfully appointed mahant, filed a suit for possession of the Dena and the properties attached to it. The suit was decreed by the trial court. The defendant filed an appeal to the High Court. The High Court held that the appellant had no knowledge about the date of the death of Som Dass and that the appellant was entitled to manage the properties of the Deta at Landeka. The High court held that after the death of the Som Dass, Shiam Dass was elected to be the Mahant of the Die. Som Dass was sued in his capacity as mahant of that Dera. The High ' Court held that after Som Dass died, the interest devolved upon Shiam Dass by virtue of law 490 or custom and that the appeal could be continued against the appellant within the time prescribed by law. The High Curt held that after S.R. 10(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, the suit was not barred by limitation. The High, Court held that since the appellant was a mahant, he was entitled to continue in possession of the properties of Dera. Som Dass, the defendant was entitled to management of the properties. The High " Court further held that the suit was barred by limitation and dismissed the suit. The appellant filed a second appeal to this Court. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The appellant was the lawfully nominated mahant of a Dera. In the absence of any certainty as to the person who would become the mahant by virtue of the law 490 or customs that there would be devolution of interest in the subject matter of the suit, the rule that has to be applied is Order 22, rule 10 notwithstanding that the period of limitation for impleading them has expired. [520G H] 2. The rule that has been applied is Order 21, rule 10, notwithstanding that the limitation for impleading the persons who would become a mahant by election has expired. The rule is based on the principle that trial of a suit cannot be brought to an end merely because the interest of a party in the subject suit has devolved upon another during the pendency of a suit but that suit may be continued against him during the pendency o suit but that it may be continued Against the person acquiring the interest with the leave of the Court. [521B] 3. The fact that it was after Som Dass was died, that he was lawfully appointed mahants of the Dia can make no difference when we are dealing with the question whether the devolution takes place as a consequence of death or for any other reason. [522C] 4. The fact of S.R., 10(1), that S.R, 10(1)(a) of the Civil Procedure Code, 1908, was applicable to the facts of the case. [523D] 5. The fact, that it was during Som Dass that Shiam Dass died, was not the subject matter in the suit but that the appeal was sought to be continued against Shiam Dass, Order 22, Rule 10 will apply(1). [523C] 6. The appellant had no right to recover possession of the property of the Dio. Som Dass. The appellant could be added as parties under Order 22, rules 10 notwithstanding that he was elected to the mahant of it. [524D] 7. The fact is that it was later on that the appellant as the lawfully appointed mujari of the Dina Dass was elected as mahant. The appellant did not have any right to recover the possession of the suit properties of the dia.

The petitioners were employees of the Andhra Pradesh State Road Transport Corporation (hereinafter referred to as the Corporation) and were governed by the Andhra Pradesh Public Service Commission (hereinafter referred as the 'Commission') Regulations, 1979. The petitioners were appointed as Assistant Engineers in the Corporation on October 29, 1979. They were confirmed in the service of the Corporation on November 30, 1979. On the basis of the recommendations of the Commission, the Government of Andhra Pradesh issued a notification dated October 29, 1980 reducing the age of retirement from 58 to 55. The petitioners challenged the said notification on the ground that it is unreasonable and arbitrary in the circumstances of the case. The petitioners contended that the reduction of the age of superannuation from 58 to 58 years was arbitrary and unreasonable in the circumstances. The petitioners also contended that the Government had acted unreasonably in not giving any previous notice to the employees which would have enabled them to arrange their affairs on the eve of retirement. The petitioners further contended that the said recommendation was accepted by the Government and consequently the age of the retirement was raised to 58 with effect from October 29,1979. The petitioners submitted that the reduction was arbitrary and illegal in the circumstances and that the decision of the Government is bad for a total non application of mind to the relevant facts and circumstances bearing on the fixation of the age. The petitioners, however, contended that the decision taken by the Government is arbitrary and unreasonable and that the Government was estopped from reducing the age from 55 to 58 years. The petitioners therefore contended that the question of the age was not referred to the Commission and that the decisions taken by the State Government are bad for a complete non application of minds to the relevant fact and circumstances bearing upon the question of age of retirement. Dismissing the petitions, ^ HELD: 1. The proviso which conferred a benefit upon Government servants by protecting their conditions of service, cannot be amended so as to empower the Government to alter those conditions to their prejudice and, in any event, they cannot be amended retrospectively so as to take away rights which had accrued to them. [723C] 2. The proviso is not arbitrary or unreasonable in the circumstance of the case and it is not unreasonable in the situation of the case, it is not arbitrary and unreasonable. [724C] 3. The proviso, which conferred a power upon the Government to amend the Fundamental Rules, cannot be modified so as to enable the Government to altered those conditions to its prejudice and, therefore, it is unreasonable in the facts and circumstances of the cases bearing on the question of fixing the age of Retirement from 58 to 60 years. [725E] 4. The proviso confers a benefit upon the Government servants by safeguarding their conditions of Service, that is, the proviso which conferred an benefit upon Government servant by protecting their condition of service, which could be taken away, if at all, only from future entrants to the Government service. [726F] 5. The proviso does not confer a benefit upon a Government servant by safeguarding their rights which had already accrued to them, if at any time, only from past entrants to Government service. The proviso merely confers a benefit on Government servants by withdrawing their conditions of their service, and does not confer any benefit upon Government employees by protecting their rights which have already accrued to him. [727F] 6. The proviso cannot be amended to the Fundamental Rules so as to empowering the Government to reduce the age of retire from 58 to58 years. [761G] 7. The proviso has no relevance to the present decision of the State to reduce the retirement of Government employees to 55 years. [758G] 8. The proviso to Article 309 read with Article 313 of the Constitution is not arbitrary, unreasonable or unreasonable in nature. [728G] 9.

The words "purchase value of goods" in section 24(2) are not words in art. They are words in art and are not words used in art. The word "sale" in section 25(2) is not used in art and the word "sale " in section 25 is not used therein. [727C] 1:6 The words "taxes" in section 23(1)(c) are not used in the art. The expression "taxes on the purchase of goods" is used in art, and the word 'sale" in art. [728C] 1.:727A] 1.8 The words " taxes" in art (a)(i) and (ii) are words in Art. 286(1)(f) and are not expressions used in art (1)(f). The appellant who was a registered dealer under the Bombay Sales Tax Act, 1947, was assessed to purchase tax on the sale of the goods in the course of export. The appellant contended that the goods remained the sellers ' property till the goods had crossed the customs barrier and thus entered the export stream, and that the sales were exempt from tax under article 286(1)(b) of the Constitution. Held, that the words " a person " in section 10(b) of Bombay Sales Tax (Amendment) Act, 1947 were wide enough to include a person " who has given such certificate under section 8(b) only if the goods were not 'despatched outside the State of Bombay within the prescribed period by anybody. The words " a registered dealer " were wide enough and could not be construed as giving a restricted meaning to the words "a person " in the section. The words ' a person " were wide and could not have been intended to include a registered dealer. The words were wide enough. The words used in section 10 of the Bombay Sales tax Act were wide enough, and could not mean that the goods were intended to be despatched by a person to whom he has sold the goods. The words in section 10 (b) of that Act were wide and did not mean that they were intended to cover a person who is not a registered dealer as sufficient. The words meant that the goods should be the property of the licensee at the time of the export. The words did not mean the goods were despatched by him or by a person who has given the certificate under section 9(b) but that they were despatched by some person who is a registered dealer to whom he sells the goods. In the present sales the goods were delivered by the purchasing dealer to the buyer at the time when they crossed the customs barriers and thus the sales were exempted from tax under section 8 of the Bombay Act. The words of section 10(a) of the Bombay General Sales Tax Act were wide in their ordinary sense and could not therefore be construed as having been used in the sense of the words " an intention and that it was the intention of the Legislature to levy purchase tax on a person who had given such certificate. The words must be construed as including the words " the buyer, at the time the export". The words " an " registered dealer " and the words " registered dealer" were wide enough in their ordinary meaning and could not, therefore, be construed as referring to the words ' a registered dealer ' and the words used in the section must be construed in the sense in which they were used in the context in which they have been used in section 8. The words are wide enough and do not mean that it was intended to cover an individual person who is neither a registered dealer nor a registered dealer, but that it was only the intention of Parliament to levy purchase duty on a person whose goods were not despatched by him. The words cannot be construed as meaning merely the words used by the Legislature. The words have to be construed as excluding the words used. The words do not mean the words used but only the words used and not the words used, and the words must be interpreted in the sense that they are used in the ordinary sense. The words may be construed as indicating the intention of legislature. The words, therefore, must be construed to mean that the legislature intended that the declaration as regards intention of the goods being despatched outside the State. The words should be construed as specifying only an intention and not that the declaration should declare only an intention. The words therefore must be construed so as to include the words used which are not intended to cover the person who is to be a registered dealer and the words should be interpreted in their ordinary and ordinary sense.

The respondent, a tenant in a building, filed a suit for eviction of the tenants on the ground that the buildings on the land leased under exhibit P 1 had also been conveyed to the LIC and that the LIC was entitled to seek fixation of fair rent in respect of the premises covered by exhibit P 1. The Rent Controller, on appeal, held that the Rent Controller had no jurisdiction to entertain the application for fixation of fair rents in respect of this premises also. The High Court, on appeal by the tenant, set aside the order of the Rent Controller and held that the order of eviction passed by the Rent Controller was not a decree in favour of the landlord. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the tenants that the Rent Control Act, was not applicable to the premises covered under exhibit P1 and that the Rent controller had no juris diction to fix the fair rent in regard thereto and that, therefore, the claim in the suit for arrears of rent based on the Rent Controller 's order in respect of that premises also had to fail. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The Rent Controller had jurisdiction to entertain a collateral attack on the validity of binding nature or correctness of the order of a Court of Small Causes and to consider and determine afresh the issue as to whether the applicant is a tenant in or landlord of, the building and (2) what the fair rent is and then fades out of the picture. [501B] 1.2 The Rent Controller has no jurisdiction to decide a question of title merely because the question may have had to be considered by the Rent Control Court as a collateral issue in deciding certain applications before them. [502C] 1.3 The Rent Controller is not competent to go into a question of Title merely because the questions may have had been to be considered before him. [503B] 1:4. The Rent Control Act is a selfcontained code and the Rent Controller has to decide whether the applicant was a tenant in, or landlord of the building and, therefore, impliedly excluded from the purview of the civil court. [505B] 1.:5. The Rent controller has to deal with this incidentally but this is not one of the direct issues before the Rent Controller. If, and only if, this relationship exists between the parties, the Rent Controller steps in for a limited purpose to determine what the fair rents is and then foades out of picture. If, the civil court in this case had come to the conclusion that there is a relationship of landlord and a tenant and that the LIGIPF policy is not ryoti land, it will have to pass a decree in respect of such premises also. [508C] 1:5. The question on which the jurisdiction of the civil courts is excluded is only the determination as to the fair rent of the premises. If, however, the civil courts in this case have come to the con sideration, it will not be open to the civil court to re determine the fair rent payable by the tenant to the landlord because that is a matter squarely and exclusively within the jurisdiction of a Rent Controller. [509D] 1.6 The Rent Controller and the High Court have jurisdiction to entertain any suit by the defeated party. [510E] 1.7 The Rent Controller have jurisdiction to decide the question as to whether there is a relation of landlord and tenant and that a civil court cannot be barred from examining a claim of title merely on the basis of the fair rent fixed by the Rent controller. [512E] 1:8. The Rent Recovery Officer has no jurisdiction, therefore, expressly excluded from the ambit of the civil Court 's jurisdiction.

In appeal to this Court, it was contended that the cost price of the packing was not includible in the assessable Value. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The cost of packing envisaged in section 4(4)(d)(i) of the Act for determining the "value" in relation to any excisable goods is only the "cost of such pack ing" incurred by the manufacturer when the packing was supplied by the assessee to the assessee. The cost price of such packing is not the cost of price of the goods, but is the cost of pack ing which is of a durable nature and returnable by the buyer to the assessee, and is returnable by the assessee. [429G] 2. The cost cost of packing contemplated in section 4 (4)(d) of the Central Excises & Salt Act, 1944, while determining the value of such goods, is only the cost of cost of such packaging which is of durable nature, and is ordinarily returnable by the manufacturer to the assessee in respect of all other costs of packing, the cost of which the goods are sold at the factory gate is to be added in the assessable price if necessary, by addition to the sale price, except where the packing is of duisable nature and returnable to the manufacturer. The cost for packing envisaged in Section 4(4) (d)(i), is repugnant to the very scheme of section 4. [430G] 3. The cost referred in section 4 of the Act, for determining the assessable value, is only a cost of such Pack ing which is returnable by a buyer to the asses see to the buyer, in respect of each other costs of pack ing. [431B] 4. The cost to be added is only the costs of such packing where the packing was either manufactured by him or is purchased or purchased by the manufacturer or by the supplier to the assessee or the purchaser. The cost, of packing, whether incurred by the assessee in packing, is attributable to the manufacturer when he sells the manufactured goods on the market. [432C] 5. The cost in respect of packing, is not the "cost" of packing, but is a "cost of the packing" incurred by him when the packing becomes returnable by the purchaser to the assessee and not the manufacturer. [433C] 6. The cost is relatable to the cost of a packing which is returnable to the assessee when the packing falls within the ambit of the cost of Packing. [434D] 7. The cost incurred by the appellant in packing, cannot be included in its assessable value when the packing occurs in packed condition. [435C] 8.

The appellant was convicted under section 161 I.P.C. and was sentenced to undergo R.I. for 15 months under section 5(2) read with section 5(1)(d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The conviction under section 161 Cr.P.c. and section 5(3) of the Act are not attracted on the proved facts. The presumption created by the provision cannot be said to be rebutted. [723C] The presumption created under the provision cannot, therefore, be held to be rebutted merely by reason of the fact that the explanation offered by the accused is reasonable and probable. it must further be shown that the explanation is a true one. [724C] The appellant had even by preponderance of probability succeeded in rebutting the presumption. [726C] The plea that clause (d) of section 5(I) of the Criminal Law Amendment Act is not attracted on th proved facts is also not impressive. [727C] The mere fact that the appellant had returned the loan and that he had given the money for the Dipawali does not mean that the explanation given by the appellant is reasonable and the presumption created by section 114 of Evidence Act and cannot be held to have been rebutted. [761D] The appellant has not even by preponderance o probability succeeded in establishing that the appellant was guilty. [728C] The prosecution has not even established that the appellant has even by preponderance Of probability succeeded in proving that the appellant received a sum of money which was not due to him as a legal remuneration.

The High court of Bombay, however, held that the term 'officer or employee ' used in sub section (1) of section 630 of the Act must be construed to mean not only the present officers and employees of a company but also to include past officers and employees, and that the phrase 'any such property ' used in cl. (a) of sub section (2) of section 634 of the Act would be rendered nugatory by projecting cl. (b) as applicable to such property of a company. The High ' Court of Bombay in Amritlal Chum vs Devi Ranjan Jha & Anr., held that it refers only to the existing officers and employees and not to former officers and employees. It is the wrongful withholding of such property, meaning the property of the company after termination of his employment. which is an offence under section 630(l)(b) of the Act, as rightly pointed out by V.S. The Court negatived the contention that the words 'any such person ' used in clause (a) and (b) of section 629 of the Act were referable to existing officers and employee ' and not to latter officers and employees while cl. (c) of sub Section (1) was attracted only to the present officers or employees and that the words "any such property" used in cl.(a) of section 642 of the Act did not extend to past officers and employee. The Court further held that the words used in cl(a) of the section 630(1) of the Income tax Officer ' used in the sub section (I) of section 628 of H 172 of the Act are referable to existing officer or employee of a company and not to old officers and employees or if such officer or employee either (a) wrongfully obtains possession of any property of the Company or (b) wrongfully withholds possession of it after the termination of his service. The Court also held that the phrase "any such person" occurring in sub section(1) was referable to existing authorities and not to the former officers and employee of a Company.

The petitioner was arrested and was detained in jail in execution of a warrant of arrest issued under section 13 of the Bombay City Land Revenue Act, 1876 for the recovery of the demand certified under section 46(2) of the Indian Income tax Act. The petitioner contended that the first part of section 46(1) of the Bombay Provincial Land Revenue Act was violative of article 14 of the Constitution and that the second part of section 13 of that Act was violative Of article 14 of Constitution. The Additional Collector of Bombay issued a recovery certificate to the Additional Collector of the Bombay, who issued the recovery certificate to him. The Additional Commissioner of Bombay, on the 8th June 1955, confirmed the recovery certificate. The petitioner filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the recovery certificate on the ground that the second portion of section 46 (2) of that Act violated article 14 of, the Constitution. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. The petitioner then filed a writ appeal in the Supreme Court. The petitioner challenged the validity of section 46 of the Bombay Presidency Land Revenue Act by special leave. The High court dismissed the writ appeal. The petitioner thereafter filed a writ application in the Supreme court. The petitioner also challenged the validity and correctness of the recovery order on the ground of discrimination. The petitioner was convicted and sentenced to imprisonment for two years. The High, Court held that section 46(3) of the Act was violative and that section 46 (3) of that act was violative of Article 14 of the constitution. The petitioner appealed to this Court. HELD: The provisions of section 46 are mutatis mutandis to be read into section 46(4) of the, Bombay City Land Tax Act, 1876. [157 D] The provisions of all the State laws are mutatis mutandis, to be read in section 46(5) of the said Act. [157 E] The provisions in section 46 (5) of that section are mutatis mutandis with respect to the recovery of arrears of land revenue. [157 F] The provisions are mutatis mutandis applicable to the recovery and recovery of arrears. [157 G] The provisions relating to recovery of arrears are certainly a territorial classification which is based on an intelligible differentia and the subjection, for the purposes of the recovery of each such class of defaulters to the same coercive process devised by their own State, on a consideration of local needs, for the recovery, of their own public demands, cannot be regarded as bereft of a reasonable nexus or correlation between the basis of classification and the object sought to be achieved by the Indian Income Tax Act any more than it can be so regarded with respect to that particular State law. [157 H] The provisions contained in section 46 are equally applicable to the Union of India, the State laws prescribe the procedure for the recovery and collection of the arrears of land tax. [157 C] The provisions regarding recovery of arrears and clothes the Collector with the power to apply either of the two methods, that is to say, he may issue a warrant of Arrest under section 13, but he is not, under the proviso, to have all the powers a Civil Court has under the Code. The provisions of sections 46 and 47 are mutatis mutandis apply to the Union, so that defaulters are treated differently in different States. [157 B] The provisions under sections 46 and 46 are mutatis materia to section 46(7) of the Income tax Act, and they are not, in terms and by themselves, concerned at all with the recovery of their own Public demands, cannot complain of denial of equal protection of the laws on the ground as the difference in mode of recovery prevailing in other States can be so treated with respect to different State laws.

[727 D] (9) The provisions, in the Calcutta Thiaka Tenancy Act, 1948 as amended by this Act were subject only to the provisions relating to notices in section 4 and not otherwise. The appellant was appointed as a Section Officer in the pay scale of Rs.400 750 and ten posts in the scale of Rs,500 1,000. The pay scale of the post of Bench Secretaries was Rs.500 1,500. The appellant was appointed to the post of Section Officer in pay scale of pay Rs.500 750. The pay scales of the post were revised by the Government by order dated January 1, 1986. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the order dated January 21, 1986. In the writ petition, the appellant contended that the classification made under the Rules was violative of the constitutional right of equal pay for equal work. The High Court rejected the writ petition. The appellant contended that it was permissible to have two scales of pay in the same cadre for persons having same duties and responsibilities. The High court held that it was not permissible to have three grades with different pay scales. The appellant preferred an appeal to this Court. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The principle of "equal pay for equal Work has to be understood in the first place. One cannot deny that often the difference is a matter of degree and that there is an element of value judgment by those who are charged with the administration in fixing the scales of pay and other conditions of service. If it has a rational nexus with the object to be sought for, as reiterated before a certain amount of value judgment has to be left with them and it cannot be interfered with by the Court unless it is demonstrated that either it is irrational or based on no basis or arrived mala fide either in law or in fact. [319C] 2. The principle laid down in the Rules is that in comparison to Bench Secretaries, the Section Officers of the secretariat have to bear more responsibilities in their Section and have to control over its subordinates. [321B] 3. The classification made under Rule framed by the Chief Justice for the purpose of entitlement to higher pay scale is not violative of the right to have equal pay for Equal work. [322C] 4. The classification is not violative either of the right of equal work. If it is irrational and based on no evidence or arrived mala fides either in law, or in fact, it is irrational. [323D] 5. The classification makes a proper classification for the purpose o entitlement to higher salary scale. The classification cannot be said to be violative of the Right to have equal work. [423E] 6. The entitlement to higher scale of pay is therefore, not on the basis of seniority alone but on the basis that merit will be evaluated by a competent authority. [424F] 7. The classification of Bench Secretaries with Grade I and Grade II is not violative. [425F] 8. The classification under the Rules, therefore, cannot be said so as to be violative Of the right to equality guaranteed under Article 14 of the Constitution. [426G] 9. The classification, therefore, must be held to be violative. [327G] 10. The classification must be held not violative of Article 14 of Constitution. [328G] 11. The classification has to be made in the first instance. The classification should be made in accordance with the Rules.

The appellant challenged the validity of the Act on the ground that the Act was not in any way repugnant to the provisions of the Act of 1973. The High Court held that the Act did not apply to the appellant and that the appellant was incompetent to exercise the powers of the Municipality under section 127A of the Municipalities Act and that the imposition of property tax was invalid. The appellant contended that the Act had no application to the appellant. The High court held that the appellant had waived its power of taxation by that agreement and, therefore, the imposition of the property tax was valid. The appellant appealed to this Court. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The Act does not provide for the constitution of the special areas and as from the date the Special Area Development Authority undertakes the functions under clause (vi) of section 68 cease to exercise the power and perform the function and duties which the Special Area Authority is competent to exercise and perform under the Act of 1972. [520 E] The Act does provide for the establishment of special areas and the functions of the special Area Development Authorities. The power conferred by the Act on Special Area Development Authorities to impose property tax on lands and buildings is therefore not in conflict with the power conferred by section 69(d) of the Act. [521 E] The power conferred under section 127(d) is not in conflictwith the power conferred under the Coal Mines Nationalisation Act on the Union Government to regulate and develop the Coal mines so as to ensure rational and scientific utilisation of coal resources. The power of the State under Entry 24, List II, is eroded only to the extent to which control was assumed by the Union Government pursuant to the declaration made by the Parliament in respect of a declared industry and that the field occupied by such enactment was the measure of the erosion of the legislative competence of the State legislature. [522 F] The power of taxation under section 127 A(2) of the Municipalities act and section 135 of the Municipal Corporation Act, 1956, is therefore not outside the conflict with the powers conferred by the Coal Mines Mines Nationalisation Act. [623 C] The power to levy property tax on land and buildings is thus not in conflict. [624 E] The property tax is imposed by respondent 1 under section 127 of the Municipalities Acts and section 135, of the Municipal Corporations Act, 1956 and section 135. The power to impose property taxes on lands and building is therefore not within conflict with the provisions of section 69(D) of the Madhya Pradesh Municipal Corporation Act. [723 E] The appellant was incompetent under section 127B of the Municipalities (Amendment) Act, 1976. [724 C] The property taxes are imposed by respondent I under section 127AA of the Municipalities and section 135 and the Municipal Corporation, Notified Area Committee or a Panchayat, as the case may be, under the Madhya Madhya Pradesh Municipalities (Amendment and Validation) Act, 1977. [725 A] The power under section 127 B of the Municipalities is thus not outside the purview of the Act and that it is not in any manner defeated by the legitimate exercise of taxing power under section 69(g) of the State Act.

The appellant was granted a lease of a certain land in the year 1945, for a period exceeding one year. The lease was for a period of one year. It was for a term exceeding one year, and the lease was for one year. On July 1, 1945, the appellant was granted the lease for a period not exceeding one year and the lease period was for a further period exceeding one years. The lease period was extended from time to time. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the lease. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. The appellant contended that the lease was not for a period beyond one year and that the lease had been granted subsequent to July 1, 1946, and that as the lease was in for a period less than one year, it was not enforceable against the Government, according to the second proviso to section 20(1) of the Abolition Act. Held, that the lease in favour of the appellant could only be terminated in accordance with the conditions laid down in the third proviso, for other wise the provisions of sub section (2) which provide for compensation will not be attracted. The words " such rights " in the third Proviso have reference to the rights created after July 1, 1944, and on that construction, the lease in question could only be done under the third proviso. The words ' such rights ' in the third provisos have reference to rights created after the 1st July, 1945, and on the construction, the term 'foregoing proviso has reference to the right created after July1, 1945, as against the Government without any further necessity for any overt act to be done by the Government to avoid the same. The words used in the third clause of the second proviso are not intended to be super imposed on the right of the Government to terminate the rights created before July 1, 1943, but only voidable at the instance of the Government. The words, ' such rights' in the third part of the second Proviso are not intended, to be superimposed on the right created before the notified date but only voidable. The words are not intended for any overt acts to be done on the right to the Government and that being the position, the Government must comply with the conditions prescribed in the third sub section. The words of the second provisos relate to the rights mentioned in the second proviso, that is to say, rights created after August 1, 1945 for a period period exceeding oneyear would be valid and enforceable by the Government against the person in whose favour such right had been created by reason of section 20(2). The words 'such rights ' in section 20(3) are not intended only to mean rights created after October 1, 1945 but also to those rights created after that date. The words in the third limb of the second part of the third proviso are not meant to be super impose on the right which was created after July. The words cannot be super imposed upon the right created by a landholder on or after the 1 st July, 1945. The words must be super imposed only on the right conferred after July 1. 1945, and not to those rights which were created after July, 1, 1945. [47C D] The words 'or such rights ' must be superimposed upon the right of Government to terminate such rights. The words were not intended to mean that rights created after September 1, 1945 could only be exercised under the third part. The words have reference to those rights. The intention of the legislature was that the creation of rights after July 1 1945, for the period exceeding one month would be valid, and enforceable by reason of the second sub section.
